title: Bondage and Beta Male Sexuality

jokes.text: Please help me seduce Britta now that you've finished doing it with her.
jokes.setup: Duncan asks Jeff for help with something, framing it as a request from one friend to another.
jokes.punchline: The request is shockingly blunt — asking his friend to help him pursue his friend's ex while explicitly referencing that the friend slept with her.
jokes.explanation: Duncan's complete lack of shame and his matter-of-fact delivery is entirely character-specific — this is exactly who he is. The bluntness is the joke. Well-constructed and economical.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Prepare to stop respecting me.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: What? Why?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Because I'm about to do something really stupid.

jokes.text: Have you met the women that do like me, Jeff? Neither have I, but trust me, they're bad people.
jokes.setup: Jeff questions whether Duncan actually likes Britta or just likes her because she doesn't like him.
jokes.punchline: Duncan concedes the point but pivots to self-deprecating logic: the women who DO like him are hypothetically terrible people he hasn't even encountered.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines of the episode. The two-part structure is perfect: acknowledging he hasn't met these women (self-aware) then confidently asserting they're bad people anyway (absurdist self-loathing). It's deeply character-specific — Duncan's particular brand of self-aware dissolution. The 'Neither have I' beat is what makes it exceptional; that half-beat of admission before the absurd pivot is structurally immaculate. Comparable in quality to the 8.0 anchor and arguably surpasses it in character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I like women who don't like me. I've never actually met a woman who likes me, but I'm pretty sure they'd be bad people.

jokes.text: Jeff's elaborate Britta-seduction strategy: grab a free hippie paper, go to the calendar page, find a cause so tragic... 'Are you writing this down?'
jokes.setup: Jeff agrees to help Duncan pursue Britta and starts laying out a calculated strategy.
jokes.punchline: 'Are you writing this down?' — Jeff is so certain in his cynical manipulation playbook that he checks whether Duncan is keeping notes, revealing how coldly transactional his view of romance is.
jokes.explanation: Classic Jeff: the joke is that his dating advice is a cold, cynical algorithm and he delivers it like a consultant. The 'are you writing this down?' is the perfect button — it escalates his self-seriousness to absurd levels.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I'm going to crash a movie premiere in costume.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: But first, I need to redesign the costume. The proportions are all wrong.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: This is a serious issue that nobody's talking about.

jokes.text: I'm gonna crash the premiere of the Kickpuncher reboot dressed like classic Kickpuncher. They shouldn't have redesigned that costume.
jokes.setup: Everyone is sharing Friday night plans after a school committee meeting.
jokes.punchline: Abed's plan is to attend a movie premiere in character-accurate protest costume, treating a franchise costume redesign with the gravity of a genuine political grievance.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Abed joke. The deadpan conviction — 'They shouldn't have redesigned that costume' — is his entire worldview: fictional canon matters as much as real-world causes. Works especially well in context because everyone else is discussing children with cleft palates.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: You actually care about this cause?

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: Oh, I'm sorry, I didn't realize that wanting to help people was such a suspicious character trait.

jokes.text: Well, it's starving children with cleft palates, Britta. What part would you have me be disinterested in?
jokes.setup: Britta expresses surprise that Duncan is interested in the charity event for starving children with cleft palates.
jokes.punchline: Duncan responds with mock indignation, pretending his only motivation is altruism by rhetorically asking which part of the cause one could possibly object to — when his actual motive is seducing Britta.
jokes.explanation: The joke layers well: the specificity of 'starving children with cleft palates' as an unobjectionable cause makes the performative indignation funnier. Duncan's faux-righteous delivery masks transparent manipulation.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Wait, if they fix the cleft palate, doesn't that mean they can eat normally? So we'd actually be putting them out of a job?

jokes.text: Kids with cleft palates should have extra food, not less. I'm in.
jokes.setup: Various study group members are agreeing to attend the benefit show.
jokes.punchline: Shirley's reasoning — 'extra food, not less' — is so self-evidently obvious that stating it as a justification is the joke. It's tautological compassion.
jokes.explanation: A quick, well-delivered character beat. Shirley's earnest moral tautology is funny precisely because she means it completely sincerely. Good economy, doesn't overstay its welcome.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I need help.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Oh, you need charity? Jeff, you should start a GoFundMe for yourself.

jokes.text: Jeff says 'I have... dinner plans' and the group reacts with open mockery — 'Yeah, make sure it's a hearty meal,' 'Oh, boo.'
jokes.setup: Everyone enthusiastically agrees to attend the charity benefit. Jeff is conspicuously silent, then offers a transparently flimsy excuse.
jokes.punchline: The group immediately sees through the excuse and piles on with sarcastic commentary, turning Jeff's selfishness into a communal roast.
jokes.explanation: Classic Jeff caught being selfish, with the group response being the payoff. The 'make sure it's a hearty meal' is a solid sardonic button. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: The play was clearly about the human condition. The man climbing the ladder represented man's struggle against society. The woman in red was a metaphor for passion. And the bird at the end... that was obviously death.

jokes.text: 'Pfft, are you really the one that needs help here, Winger?' / 'Yeah, should we write a check to the Jeff Foundation?'
jokes.setup: Jeff asks for help defending himself from the group's criticism about not wanting to attend the charity event.
jokes.punchline: Annie and Troy immediately pile on with 'The Jeff Foundation' joke — framing Jeff's selfishness as a charitable cause in itself, requiring donations.
jokes.explanation: 'The Jeff Foundation' is a punchy, well-constructed riff — it inverts the charitable framing of the scene to skewer Jeff's narcissism. Quick and sharp.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Well, if we're deconstructing the postmodern semiotics of the text, we must consider the liminal space between signifier and signified, which inevitably invokes a Derridean framework of différance that fundamentally interrogates the hegemonic structures of canonical interpretation.

jokes.text: Post-show interpretation: 'Well, the ants were people. The Queen Ant was an oil company.' / 'Okay, so it was about our marginalized perceptions as drones being born into a corporate hive-mind?' / [beat] 'McDonald's?' / 'Oh, I was just thinking about that.'
jokes.setup: Two people earnestly analyze the deep allegorical meaning of a performance art piece about ants.
jokes.punchline: The highbrow analytical conversation is immediately punctured by someone randomly saying 'McDonald's?' — revealing that the profound discussion instantly triggered a hunger response, not existential revelation.
jokes.explanation: One of the strongest jokes in the episode. The setup is a parody of pretentious post-show analysis, then the punchline deflates it with sublime bathos — 'McDonald's?' arrives out of nowhere and the response 'Oh, I was just thinking about that' confirms it's a shared hunger response. The specificity of 'McDonald's' rather than any generic food is perfect. The 'Mm-hmm, hungry' confirmation is a beautiful grace note. Tight, original, and structurally immaculate.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: You know, this reminds me of the time my uncle tried to fight a bear with a spatula. He lost both his shoes and his dignity that day. My family doesn't talk about it anymore.

jokes.text: Duncan's non-sequitur during Duncan's phone call crisis: 'Uh, my mother used to tell a story about how she killed a chicken. Hong Kong, 1964.'
jokes.setup: Duncan is having an apparently serious and emotionally fraught phone call with someone named Alessandra. The group is watching awkwardly.
jokes.punchline: Duncan, unable to process the social discomfort, randomly offers a story about his mother killing a chicken in Hong Kong in 1964 — a completely unrelated, specific, and inexplicable non-sequitur.
jokes.explanation: The specificity is everything here — 'Hong Kong, 1964' transforms a generic awkward deflection into something genuinely absurd and character-revealing. It suggests Duncan has a whole world of strange personal history. The deadpan delivery of a non-sequitur chicken story as social escape is both funny and strangely poignant. The timestamp pause after it lands suggests the camera holds on the uncomfortable silence.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Michael? That's a really respected name.

dialogue.speaker: Michael
dialogue.line: Thanks.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Yeah, you know, I've never met a Michael who wasn't doing pretty well for himself.

dialogue.speaker: Michael
dialogue.line: Oh.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: It's pronounced 'MY-kul', you know? That's a winner's pronunciation.

jokes.text: Duncan on Britta's anarchist friend Michael: 'I don't like this 'my-kale' guy. I don't think he likes himself, or he'd pronounce it 'Michael.''
jokes.setup: Britta greets an old anarchist friend whose name appears to be pronounced 'My-kale' (like the vegetable), which Duncan finds insufferable.
jokes.punchline: Duncan's snobbishness about the affected pronunciation becomes a quasi-philosophical statement — that someone with self-respect would use the standard pronunciation.
jokes.explanation: Sharp and quotable. The name-as-kale pun earns its wordplay label but the real joke is the pseudo-psychological logic Duncan applies to it. Very character-specific — Duncan's academic pomposity colliding with his petty jealousy.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: I'm attracted to Britta because she's like America. She had potential, she's still got some good qualities, but she's fundamentally declining and I have a weird fetish for that.

jokes.text: Duncan's America speech: 'She's everything I love about America. Bold, opinionated, just past her peak, and starting to realize that she has to settle for less.'
jokes.setup: Duncan watches Britta and compliments her to Jeff, using 'America' as a framing device.
jokes.punchline: The 'compliment' reveals itself as a barely-veiled patronizing assessment — 'just past her peak, starting to realize she has to settle for less' — which is both a devastating character observation and self-serving, since Duncan IS the 'settling for less.'
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The 'America' framing is a clever misdirect — it sounds like a broader observation but becomes a specific character takedown. The double edge is what makes it exceptional: it's simultaneously a compliment, an insult to Britta, and self-incriminating (Duncan is the 'less' she'd be settling for). The political metaphor (America past its peak, settling) adds a satirical layer. Structurally near-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Michael
dialogue.line: This is Britta, she's a hero. She's always fighting for what's right.

dialogue.speaker: Michael
dialogue.line: I've been trying to be more like her, you know? Really making a difference.

dialogue.speaker: Michael
dialogue.line: But honestly, I'm just imitating it. I'm not actually doing any of it.

jokes.text: Jeff leaving Duncan to circle Britta: 'Have fun circling my former lover, waiting for her to cry. I tried to make that sound good, but that's what you're doin'.'
jokes.setup: Jeff decides to leave, ceding the field to Duncan's pursuit of Britta.
jokes.punchline: Jeff bluntly summarizes what Duncan is actually doing — 'circling my former lover, waiting for her to cry' — catches himself trying to frame it diplomatically, then gives up and confirms the grim truth anyway.
jokes.explanation: The self-correction structure ('I tried to make that sound good, but...') is what elevates this. It acknowledges the writer's room's own joke, making it meta without being too cute. Very Jeff — the moment of attempted spin followed by honest resignation is pitch-perfect. 'Circling my former lover, waiting for her to cry' is a genuinely quotable, vivid phrase.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Oh, well, I appreciate that, but I'm not really a hero. I just have a degree in psychology from... well, several places, actually. The point is, you shouldn't listen to anyone, including me. Especially not me. In fact, if I tell you to do something, do the opposite.

jokes.text: Michael introduces Britta as 'the bravest, most passionate activist I have ever had the honor of imitating.'
jokes.setup: Michael is introducing Britta as a hero at the benefit event, using the standard format of effusive praise.
jokes.punchline: '...the honor of imitating' — instead of the expected 'working alongside' or 'knowing,' he says 'imitating,' revealing that his activism is performative mimicry of real people like Britta.
jokes.explanation: Smart single-word subversion. 'Imitating' instead of an expected word like 'knowing' or 'working with' does enormous comedic work — it simultaneously undercuts Michael and ironically elevates Britta. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: Why are you staying for a drink?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Alcoholism.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: It has to be genuine.

jokes.text: Britta's speech: 'Oh. Wow, um, I'm not a hero. I'm a high school dropout and a bartender, so don't listen to me. Or anyone. Just listen to yourself, and make sure you tell yourself the truth.'
jokes.setup: Britta is put on the spot at the activist benefit and asked to say something inspiring.
jokes.punchline: She starts by deflecting, escalates the deflection to 'don't listen to me. Or anyone.' — which accidentally becomes profound advice — then pivots to something that sounds like genuine wisdom. The joke is that Britta stumbles into an actually good inspirational speech while trying to disqualify herself.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Britta. Her self-deprecation escalates to 'don't listen to anyone' which is both a joke and unexpectedly good advice. The joke works on multiple levels: it satirizes activist posturing, Britta's self-sabotage, and accidentally produces genuine insight. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Cool. Cool cool cool cool cool.

jokes.text: Duncan pressing Britta to stay: 'Why?' / Britta: 'I like to drink.' / Duncan: 'Oh, really?' / Britta: 'Yeah. I have a serious problem.' / Duncan: 'That had better be true.'
jokes.setup: Duncan tries to get Britta to stay for a drink and asks why she would.
jokes.punchline: Britta's admission that she has a 'serious problem' with drinking is treated by Duncan not with concern but with hopeful enthusiasm — 'That had better be true' — because her dysfunction is what makes her appealing/available to him.
jokes.explanation: 'That had better be true' is an excellent button. It's dark, honest about Duncan's predatory hope, and weirdly endearing. The two-beat delivery (Britta admits the problem, Duncan confirms he WANTS it to be a problem) is well-structured. High character integration for both.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I am Kickpuncher. Crime-fighting through the power of kicking... and punching. HYAH!

jokes.text: Jeff's 'Cool. Cool, cool, cool.' — said to himself after being shamed into attending the benefit.
jokes.setup: Jeff has just been guilted into attending the charity event against his will.
jokes.punchline: His repeated 'cool' is the verbal equivalent of a resigned shrug — the character's signature catchphrase used here to mask defeat.
jokes.explanation: One of Community's signature Abed-but-actually-Jeff catchphrase moments. The triple 'cool' is a fan-beloved verbal tic that works as a reaction beat here. Quotability is high due to its status as a show signature, but the craft of this specific deployment is functional rather than exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I can't use a glue gun. There's a whole story there, but I'm not going to tell it because it would completely upstage whatever's happening right now.

jokes.text: Abed in Kickpuncher costume: 'I am Kickpuncher. You are in violation of future law.' followed by 'Pew! Pew! Pew! Pew!' sound effects.
jokes.setup: Abed has dressed as Kickpuncher to protest the costume redesign at the film premiere.
jokes.punchline: He delivers a fully committed in-character warning and then makes laser sound effects with his mouth — the juxtaposition of total sincerity with complete absurdity.
jokes.explanation: Classic Abed — his complete commitment to the bit is the joke. 'You are in violation of future law' is a great sci-fi parody line delivered with utter conviction. The 'pew pew' mouth-laser is a visual/audio gag that works on its own.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: I'd stockpile spices. Cumin, paprika, saffron—the expensive stuff. After the apocalypse, people won't care about gold or diamonds. They'll trade their last can of beans for a pinch of real vanilla.

jokes.text: Annie banned glue guns from the apartment 'after an incident so hilarious that even describing it would narratively eclipse what's happening here.'
jokes.setup: Pierce asks what Abed is doing with a costume, and Abed explains the glue gun situation.
jokes.punchline: Abed's explanation is meta: he withholds the story because telling it would be narratively superior to the current scene — a character explicitly aware of story hierarchy and structure.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode and a quintessential Community/Abed joke. The meta-commentary on narrative economy — a CHARACTER refusing to tell a story because it would 'eclipse' the current scene — is both a clever structural gag and the most Abed thing possible. It's also a subtle joke about sitcom writing: the writers are aware they're omitting a funnier scene. Very high craft across all dimensions. The 'narratively eclipse' phrasing is pitch-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: What are you doing?

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: I'm the first person to ever discipline you.

jokes.text: Pierce's post-apocalyptic survival plan: 'I would raise goats, hoard cinnamon, and travel only at night.'
jokes.setup: Abed asks Pierce what he would do if he were a post-apocalyptic survivor.
jokes.punchline: Pierce delivers a weirdly specific and confident survival plan — the cinnamon hoarding is the key absurdist element, suggesting Pierce has thought deeply about this in a way that reveals his paranoid, self-sufficient worldview.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'hoard cinnamon' is perfect — it's not gold or ammunition, it's cinnamon — which implies a survivalist logic that's both plausible and ridiculous. Very Pierce. The rhythm of the three-part list (goats / cinnamon / night travel) is well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I'm working on my action movie script.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: Oh yeah? What's it called?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Ass Crack Bandit: The Reckoning.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: You mean 'Ass Crack Bananas'? That's a terrible name. You know what? I'm gonna make sure you miss that premiere.

jokes.text: Pierce demonstrates 'Initiate ballistic foam' — fires foam at Abed's costume and destroys five hours of work.
jokes.setup: Pierce is bonding with Abed and shows him something, saying 'watch this' with pride.
jokes.punchline: He fires a ballistic foam device — a ridiculous gadget — that completely destroys Abed's painstakingly crafted Kickpuncher costume. Pierce's delight turning to everyone's horror.
jokes.explanation: The setup-consequence structure is clean and the physical comedy lands. 'Initiate ballistic foam' as a phrase is funny on its own. Pierce's total lack of awareness about the damage makes it character-specific and not just random destruction.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: You people have turned that kid into a monster. He wants to watch TV? You all stop what you're doing. He wants to make a blanket fort? You help him build it. He wants to speak in nothing but pop culture references? You just nod along like he's Confucius.

jokes.text: Initiate ballistic foam. [foam cannon fires, destroying Abed's work]
jokes.setup: Chang wants to show Abed something — he's apparently acquired or built a foam cannon
jokes.punchline: He fires it and destroys five hours of Abed's costume work
jokes.explanation: Functional slapstick. 'Initiate ballistic foam' is a good line — the clinical activation phrase before casual destruction is funny. The setup and payoff work mechanically, though it's not a high-craft moment.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: Yeah, I've done a lot of tough stuff. I watched my third wife die.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: Didn't even flinch.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'I know this is bad timing, but I should go if I'm gonna make the movie, so...'
jokes.setup: Pierce has just destroyed Abed's costume and Abed is furious.
jokes.punchline: Pierce's response is to try to exit the situation as if normal social protocols apply — casually excusing himself — which is funnier than any direct acknowledgment of what he did.
jokes.explanation: Pierce's oblivious attempt to exit after causing chaos is a reliable character beat. 'I know this is bad timing, but...' as an understatement of epic proportions is the joke. Functional character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm gonna discipline you, and it's gonna work because nobody's ever disciplined you before.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You're like a tourist at the Great Wall of China thinking you're the first one to climb it.

jokes.text: Pierce grounding Abed: 'Something nobody ever does. Teaching you consequences.'
jokes.setup: Abed tries to leave for his movie. Pierce physically blocks him.
jokes.punchline: Pierce — who just carelessly destroyed Abed's work — now positions himself as the disciplinarian teaching consequences, with no self-awareness that HE is the one being destructive.
jokes.explanation: The irony is well-deployed. Pierce's self-appointed moral authority after causing the problem is exactly his character dynamic. The scene begins setting up a genuinely interesting bottle episode dynamic between Pierce and Abed.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That duck represents the struggle of the working class against the oppressive forces of capitalism. His name is Steven.

jokes.text: Abed to Pierce: 'And what 'kicky-punch' movie is that from? The ones you've seen or the one I'm gonna watch you miss?'
jokes.setup: Pierce is lecturing Abed about being refused something and not getting his way.
jokes.punchline: Abed flips Pierce's lecture back at him using the Kickpuncher movie — turning Pierce's moralizing into a callback to the actual stakes (missing the film). 'The ones you've seen or the one I'm gonna watch you miss' is a pointed two-part rebuttal.
jokes.explanation: Smart comeback structure. Abed weaponizes the Kickpuncher movie against Pierce's sermon in a way that's both cutting and character-true. The diminutive 'kicky-punch' adds a nice contemptuous note.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I saw an amazing performance at the community theater last night.

dialogue.speaker: Janitor
dialogue.line: That theater's been closed since the fire in '09. Twelve people died.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Well, they were very committed to their craft.

jokes.text: 'I'm sorry I punched my landlord, but I'm not gettin' my deposit back.'
jokes.setup: Pierce is using an analogy to explain the concept of consequences to Abed.
jokes.punchline: His example of accepted punishment is that he punched his landlord and now won't get his deposit back — suggesting he punched his landlord deliberately and considers losing a security deposit a proportionate consequence.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Pierce. The casualness of 'I punched my landlord' as a philosophical example is very funny — it implies this is not unusual behavior for him and that losing a deposit is an entirely acceptable trade-off. The example completely undercuts his authority as a moral lecturer.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: I'm naturally contrarian. I don't follow trends—I actively resist them.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: So when I'm attracted to the most popular women on campus, it's not because they're popular. It's because I'm subconsciously rejecting the idea that I should be attracted to them, which makes me attracted to them.

jokes.text: Pierce's speech about Abed's eggshells: '...Everybody hide their hamburgers! If Abed sees a hamburger, we'll all travel in time. Let's eat cookies and ice cream and dress in pajamas in the middle of the day.'
jokes.setup: Pierce goes on a rant about how the whole group walks on eggshells around Abed's eccentricities.
jokes.punchline: His specific examples of 'walking on eggshells' are themselves absurd — hamburger time travel, pajama days — suggesting Pierce has been storing up genuine (if misguided) grievances about the group's indulgence of Abed.
jokes.explanation: The humor lives in the specific absurdity of Pierce's examples — hamburger time travel is a gloriously strange image. It also works as a callback to the show's history. Pierce's genuine frustration makes this more than just a list joke.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: You think you're so smooth with your romantic tactics, but you're no Jason Biggs. You're more like Dane Cook—trying way too hard and nobody's laughing.

jokes.text: 'I watched my third wife die!'
jokes.setup: Pierce is in the middle of a tirade about how the group coddles Abed, listing examples of real suffering he has endured that nobody accommodates.
jokes.punchline: He suddenly pivots to 'I watched my third wife die!' — delivered as a non-sequitur emotional outburst that is both genuinely pathetic and darkly funny. 'Third wife' does heavy lifting — implying a pattern of marriages and losses.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. Everything about this works: the sudden escalation from petty complaints about hamburgers and pajamas to genuine tragedy, the specificity of 'third wife' (not just 'wife'), the implication that he has watched at least three marriages and one death, and the complete tonal whiplash. The economy is extraordinary — four words do enormous emotional and comedic work. It's both a devastating character moment and very funny. High comparable to the vasectomy anchor example in its use of a number to amplify dark escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Wait, so you're telling me you don't remember how you got here?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I remember walking into the study room and then... nothing.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: That's exactly what happened to me too.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: We're all experiencing the same memory gap. The probability we're all just forgetful is statistically insignificant.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Oh my God. Oh my God, you guys... I don't think we're alive.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: What? That's insane!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Wait, when did we last eat? Or sleep? Or feel anything?

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Lord have mercy... he might be right.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Well, I've been dead inside for years, so this is just official paperwork.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: We're all ghosts. We're all dead.

jokes.text: Abed: 'You're not the Marco Polo of bullying me. You're just another tourist taking pictures of a great, big wall.'
jokes.setup: Pierce has just made an emotional appeal about being overlooked. Abed responds.
jokes.punchline: Abed's metaphor — Marco Polo of bullying, tourist at the Great Wall — is simultaneously cutting, pretentious in the best way, and oddly poetic. It acknowledges he has been bullied extensively before Pierce.
jokes.explanation: One of Abed's best lines in the episode. The Marco Polo / Great Wall metaphor is inventive, vivid, and reveals character depth (Abed has been here before, many times, with many people). The 'tourist taking pictures' extension is elegant. It's both a great insult and a revealing self-portrait. High originality and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Janitor
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. So you believed ghosts... about ghosts?

jokes.text: You're not the Marco Polo of bullying me. You're just another tourist taking pictures of a great, big wall.
jokes.setup: Chang claims Abed has never experienced someone controlling him
jokes.punchline: Abed's metaphor — framing himself as a Great Wall that tourists (bullies) merely visit — is both self-aggrandizing and historically incongruous in a way that's perfectly Abed
jokes.explanation: Very strong line. The Marco Polo/Great Wall metaphor is both a coherent defense mechanism and a strange piece of historical self-mythology. 'You're not the Marco Polo of bullying me' is a great sentence — the idea that someone could pioneer the discovery of bullying Abed is both absurd and weirdly compelling. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: We could totally Banksy this billboard. I'll organize it like a heist. Everyone gets a role.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Britta, Banksy is a person, not a verb.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Not with that attitude. Come on, we're going to Banksy the hell out of this thing.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'Looked like you were doodling chickens.' / Abed: 'He is a duck!' / Pierce: 'Uh-oh.'
jokes.setup: Pierce discovers Abed has been drawing and realizes he may have destroyed something important. He sees the drawings and dismisses them as chicken doodles.
jokes.punchline: Abed's emphatic correction — 'He is a duck!' — and Pierce's immediate recognition of the gravity of his error ('Uh-oh') is a perfect three-beat structure. The duck/chicken distinction is hilariously specific.
jokes.explanation: One of the most economical and well-structured jokes in the episode. Three beats, six words total for the punchline-counterpunchline-realization. 'He is a duck!' has the perfect indignant specificity of someone defending their creative work. Pierce's 'Uh-oh' perfectly encapsulates dawning horror. The humor works on the duck/chicken confusion level AND as a character revelation (Abed has a creative project). Very rewatch-able.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Nothing to lose? I have PLENTY to lose! My dignity, my self-respect, my carefully curated image as someone who's better than all of you!

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: And another thing — this kind of rhetoric is exactly what the one percent WANTS us to think. That we're expendable. That we have nothing to lose but our chains!

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: You're all just unconsciously perpetuating a system of economic oppression designed to keep the working class docile and complacent!

jokes.text: Chang claiming to have done a one-man show for an 'audience' in the abandoned theater.
jokes.setup: Security tells Chang he's not allowed in the theater.
jokes.punchline: Chang claims he just did a one-man show for a 'little audience' — but the theater has been closed since 24 people died there in 1997, so the 'audience' would have been ghosts. Chang seems completely unbothered.
jokes.explanation: Chang's oblivious confidence is well-deployed. The retroactive horror of realizing he performed for the dead is a good dark absurdist beat, though it only fully lands once the security guard explains the theater history.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Your taste in movies is objectively terrible. You watch nothing but low-budget action films and you don't even appreciate the craft.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: What? I like what I like.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Exactly. You're predictable, boring, and you have no emotional depth.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: Okay, why are you being so mean?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Because I'm trying to hurt your feelings.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: Well you did. I'm actually... kind of hurt.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Wait, really? I didn't think you had feelings.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: I didn't think YOU had feelings.

jokes.text: Security guard: '...since the 1997 fire. 24 people died.' / 'So what have you guys been up to?'
jokes.setup: The security guard explains the theater has been closed since 1997 due to a fire in which 24 people died.
jokes.punchline: Chang immediately pivots to 'So what have you guys been up to?' — treating the revelation of a mass-casualty event as a conversational formality before moving on to small talk.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Chang. The pivot from '24 people died' to casual small talk is exactly his sociopathic social obliviousness. The economy is excellent — no transition, no acknowledgment, just immediate topic change. Very character-specific. Dark and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: Your stuff isn't clever, it's just references to other stuff. You're like a human Tumblr. You've never had an original thought in your life, and frankly, watching you try to be profound is like watching a parrot recite Shakespeare.

jokes.text: Duncan's 'I hated Reese's Pieces before E.T. ate them, sorry.' confession to Jeff about his attraction to Britta.
jokes.setup: Duncan confesses that what turns him on about Britta is that everyone else likes her — he's attracted to her because she's popular, not because of her intrinsic qualities.
jokes.punchline: His analogy: he hated Reese's Pieces before E.T. made them famous — he's attracted to things based on external validation, not personal taste. It's a devastating self-indictment delivered as a casual pop culture riff.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. The E.T./Reese's Pieces reference perfectly encapsulates Duncan's psychological problem with desire — he wants what others want, not what he genuinely wants. The 'sorry' at the end is a perfect grace note of self-aware shame. Very character-specific, well-structured, and quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: His name is Buzz Hickey.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: Wait, what? You named him after me?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Well, he's the cool character.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: Oh, that's nice. So what happens to him?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: He dies in the first episode.

jokes.text: Jeff accuses Duncan of being like Dane Cook 'in one of those three movies he was in about Dane Cook getting laid by accident. Only it's not a Dane Cook movie, Jeff, because this time, someone's watching: me. Your friend, British Jason Biggs.'
jokes.setup: Duncan realizes Jeff intends to pursue Britta himself and accuses him of running a Dane Cook rom-com move.
jokes.punchline: 'British Jason Biggs' as Duncan's self-description is the gem — it's self-deprecating, accurate as a character analogy (the bumbling romantic lead), and funnier than expected. The Dane Cook dig is a secondary comedic layer.
jokes.explanation: 'British Jason Biggs' lands as a great self-applied label — it's specific, accurate, and self-aware in a way that makes Duncan oddly sympathetic. The Dane Cook framing is a bit dated but still functions.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: Hey Abed, I got something that'll cheer you up.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: It's a Dreamatorium session. You know, that thing you built?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: Yeah. It's called 'Abed's a Crybaby.' I'm gonna go in there and do an impression of you right now.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'If you never call me Dane Cook again, I'll stand down... for an hour.' / Duncan: 'Okay. An hour.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is offended at being compared to Dane Cook and negotiates with Duncan over Britta.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's 'stand down... for an hour' — with the comedic pause — reveals that his stated generosity is just temporary and tactical. 'An hour' accepted without protest acknowledges both men are operating on a transparently short-game basis.
jokes.explanation: Good beat. The specificity of 'an hour' deflates the truce instantly and both characters' immediate acceptance is funny — it shows they both know exactly what this is.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'I've been a cab driver, a soldier, a cop, but what terrifies me the most is the opinion of a manchild in cardboard pants.'
jokes.setup: Abed accuses Pierce of being afraid he won't like his duck cartoon.
jokes.punchline: Pierce lists his formidable life experiences (cab driver, soldier, cop) and then ranks Abed's potential disapproval as more terrifying — which both mocks Abed and inadvertently reveals Pierce's own insecurity about seeking approval.
jokes.explanation: 'Manchild in cardboard pants' is a vivid, well-chosen phrase. The list structure (cab driver, soldier, cop) gives good comedic rhythm before the punchline. It's both an insult and an admission, which makes it dimensional.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: If my friends were really my friends, they'd want to spend time with me. But they don't want to spend time with me. Therefore, they're not really my friends.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: But wait—if they're not really my friends, then I have no friends. And if I have no friends, then there's no one who doesn't want to spend time with me. So maybe they are my friends after all.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: But if they're my friends, then they should want to spend time with me... which brings me back to the beginning.

jokes.text: Abed: 'Kickpuncher was a cop before he became a cyborg. So you were a cop before you became... this.'
jokes.setup: Pierce has just mentioned he used to be a cop as part of his credentials.
jokes.punchline: Abed immediately maps Pierce's biography onto the Kickpuncher narrative — 'you were a cop before you became... this' — with the hanging 'this' implying a devastating assessment of Pierce's current state.
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback structure. Abed repurposes the Kickpuncher mythology as a lens on Pierce's real life, and the elliptical 'this' as an indictment of Pierce's current existence is both funny and genuinely cutting. The pause before 'this' is crucial.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I'm worthless. No, worse than worthless. I'm a net negative on the world.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: And if I'm worthless, then anyone who likes me must also be worthless, because they have bad taste.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Which means you're all worthless, so you're not really my friends—you're just other worthless people I happen to know.

jokes.text: Chang confronting the theater group: 'You're ghosts!' / Group: 'We're ghosts?' / Chang: 'The janitor out there told me you died in 1997.' — then immediately telling the security guard that the people inside told him the guard is a ghost.
jokes.setup: Chang has been told by the security guard that everyone in the theater died in 1997. He enters and accuses the living people of being ghosts.
jokes.punchline: The group's bewildered 'We're ghosts?' is beat one. Then Chang runs back out and tells the guard 'those guys in there told me that you're the one who died in a fire and you're a ghost!' — confirming Chang has been played by both sides of a prank and believes all of it.
jokes.explanation: Chang's credulous relaying of contradictory ghost accusations is very funny. His total inability to parse any of this — accepting both claims simultaneously — is perfect for his character. The structure escalates well from confusion to absurd chaos.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Thank you for not taking advantage of me last night.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: Well, I wanted to, but my car wouldn't start.

jokes.text: No, no, no, no, no! Stop that! You're ghosts! / We're ghosts?
jokes.setup: Chang confronts the people he met in the theater after learning the theater burned down with 24 deaths in 1997.
jokes.punchline: He announces they're ghosts, and they respond with apparent surprise — as if the ghosts didn't know they were ghosts — a classic Sixth Sense inversion played absurdly straight.
jokes.explanation: The gag of ghosts being unaware they're ghosts is a well-worn trope, but executed here with enough absurdist speed to work. The subsequent 'you just believed a bunch of ghosts?' reversal is what makes it pay off.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: British cars are actually quite reliable if you maintain them properly.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: It's not about the car. It's about... never mind.

jokes.text: Duncan's Consensual Perfume billboard observation: 'The one with the man chasing the woman through the grass and it says, "Proven in its field"?' / Britta: 'Yeah, proven in its field and in labs on the eyeballs of rabbits.'
jokes.setup: Duncan references a perfume billboard he noticed, apparently as an icebreaker.
jokes.punchline: Britta immediately adds the dark subtext about animal testing — 'in labs on the eyeballs of rabbits' — turning what could have been a flirtatious moment into an animal rights lecture.
jokes.explanation: Very character-specific for Britta — her ability to immediately attach a social justice caveat to any situation. The setup (Duncan trying to be charming about wordplay) versus Britta's immediate pivot to animal testing is classic Britta humor.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: So what do you think of my screenplay?

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: Well... it's certainly something.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That good, huh?

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: Look, kid. The dialogue is wooden, the pacing is off, and I have no idea what's supposed to be happening in act two. But you know what? I've seen worse. Not recently, but I've seen it. And I'm gonna help you fix this thing.

jokes.text: Yeah, proven in its field and in labs on the eyeballs of rabbits. We should make it say that! Who's got the spray paint?
jokes.setup: Britta points out the problematic perfume ad
jokes.punchline: Friend escalates by adding the animal testing angle AND immediately leaps to direct action (Banksy the billboard)
jokes.explanation: Good escalation that shows how activist energy works — one complaint becomes a mobilization event. 'On the eyeballs of rabbits' is a solid detail. The jump to 'Who's got the spray paint?' is a nice beat.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You know, Duncan, I've been thinking about what you said in class today. It really resonated with me on a deeper level.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: Are you... are you coming onto me?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: What? No! I was just trying to have a genuine moment of connection with you.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: Oh. Well, that's disappointing.

jokes.text: Duncan's reaction to the activist group proposing to spraypaint the billboard: 'No, guys, I'm serious! Doug and Janet, you're on lookout. Michael works the ladder. I will banksy that mother!'
jokes.setup: Britta's friends propose to spraypaint 'proven in labs on the eyeballs of rabbits' over the perfume billboard.
jokes.punchline: Duncan — the sellout academic who came here to pursue Britta — immediately becomes the most enthusiastic and tactically prepared member of the group, even deploying 'banksy' as a verb.
jokes.explanation: Duncan using 'banksy' as a verb while assigning military-style roles is funny and character-consistent — his competitive need to perform (here: perform activism) overrides his actual values. Good energy.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You're a good friend, Duncan.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: Thanks, Jeff. You know, I've been thinking... maybe we should make a pact. A mutual vow of celibacy.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: What? Why would we do that?

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: Well, it would bring us closer together. As friends. Spiritually.

jokes.text: Janet's response to Britta inciting the group: 'Well, that's convenient for the one with nothing to lose.'
jokes.setup: Britta gives an impassioned 'take risks again' speech to her old activist friends.
jokes.punchline: Janet punctures Britta's revolutionary fervor by pointing out that Britta is the one with no stake in the consequences — she has nothing to lose, so risk-taking is easy for her.
jokes.explanation: Sharp and true. It's a good satirical observation about performative activism and the privilege of risk-taking when you have nothing to lose. Functions both as a joke and as thematic content.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Hey Hickey, what's the difference between a .38 and a .45?

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: About a foot, once it leaves the barrel.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Perfect. I'm stealing that for my script.

jokes.text: Britta: 'Oh, so the person with the least wealth has the least valid argument? That's convenient.' / Janet: 'Britta, how many people have you fed this year besides yourself?'
jokes.setup: Britta tries to turn the attack on her into a class argument.
jokes.punchline: Janet destroys Britta's rhetorical pivot with a concrete, unanswerable question: 'How many people have you fed this year besides yourself?' — exposing Britta's activism as performative rather than practical.
jokes.explanation: One of the best Britta takedowns in the episode. The rhetorical trap — Britta tries to class-warrior her way out of criticism, gets hit with a simple practical question — is structurally elegant. It's very character-specific for both Britta (performative activism) and Janet (practical activist). The 'besides yourself' coda is well-placed.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Wait, so if I saw a ghost, how do I know the ghost was real? Maybe I'm hallucinating. But if I'm hallucinating, then the ghost isn't real, which means I didn't see a ghost, which means I'm not hallucinating. But if I'm not hallucinating, then the ghost was real!

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: So either way, I'm crazy or I'm not crazy, but I can't figure out which one because the ghost is the only evidence and the ghost might not be real because I might be crazy!

jokes.text: Oh, so the person with the least wealth has the least valid argument? That's convenient.
jokes.setup: Activist friend tells Britta she has nothing to lose, implying her argument is cheap
jokes.punchline: Britta reframes the class argument ironically — the response is structurally correct but deployed in service of convincing people to commit vandalism
jokes.explanation: Britta deploying class-consciousness rhetoric to justify misdemeanor vandalism is a good bit of hypocrisy comedy. The 'That's convenient' mirroring the previous line is a nice touch.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: The whole thing was a metaphor for the human condition.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: That's what I said!

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: No, I was there. I saw the guy in the big rubber suit. That was definitely supposed to be humanity.

jokes.text: Duncan and Britta leaving the activist group together — the implied 'yeah' and 'oh my God' reaction after the charged 'would you like to go...' moment.
jokes.setup: The activist group has essentially expelled Britta by calling out her performative activism. Duncan has been waiting for exactly this vulnerable moment.
jokes.punchline: The 'yeah? / oh my God' reaction — played as a moment of surprising mutual attraction — is immediately undercut by the audience knowing Duncan engineered this via Jeff's advice about waiting for her to cry.
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the Duncan/Britta seduction plot works as a callback payoff — Duncan's calculated waiting for the vulnerable moment pays off. The comedic irony runs underneath the apparently sweet moment.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: What if none of this is real? What if I'm just a figment of someone's imagination?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Have you tried taking a bath?

jokes.text: These are really good. It helps me to see why you were so upset. — Did I ruin anything as good as what's in here? — Ah, just practice drawings.
jokes.setup: Chang looks through Abed's sketchbook and is genuinely moved
jokes.punchline: Abed's response to earnest praise for his work is complete understatement — 'just practice drawings'
jokes.explanation: More of an emotional beat than a pure joke, but the understatement from the person who just screamed 'He is a duck!' over their honor is gently funny.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: My dad left when I was seven.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Mine never really showed up to begin with.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Yeah, well... at least you knew what to expect.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I guess we're both just... broken.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Cool. Cool cool cool.

jokes.text: I can see from the clock that if I hit all the green lights... — I'm sorry, I can't let you go. That'd undercut the larger lesson.
jokes.setup: Abed is calculating whether he can still make the movie
jokes.punchline: Chang, who accidentally destroyed Abed's work and was being taught a lesson, has now reversed roles — he's the one imposing lessons on Abed
jokes.explanation: Nice role reversal — Chang has absorbed Abed's lesson language and is now deploying it against him. 'That'd undercut the larger lesson' is Abed's exact logic returned to him. The irony is well-constructed.

jokes.text: Your cartoons are monuments to joylessness, nervously assembled jokes based on nothing from your life or anyone's life!
jokes.setup: Abed goads Chang by saying 'you have feelings, go ahead and hurt mine'
jokes.punchline: Chang's critique of Abed's cartoons is both savage and reveals genuine artistic insight — 'monuments to joylessness' is a great phrase
jokes.explanation: 'Monuments to joylessness' is a sharp phrase that works both as an insult and as a legible critique. The fact that Chang — Chang — is delivering coherent art criticism to Abed is itself funny and character-subverting. The line 'nervously assembled jokes based on nothing from your life or anyone's life' is also pointed, with an almost self-aware quality given Community's own reputation.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'In the words of your hacky duck, "What the hell?"'
jokes.setup: Abed has just delivered a devastating speech to Pierce about his cartoons being joyless and emotionally empty. After a long silence, Pierce responds.
jokes.punchline: Pierce quotes the duck ('What the hell?') as his response — which is both funny as a simple expression of bewilderment AND functions as Pierce using the duck's voice to respond to Abed's attack on the duck's creator.
jokes.explanation: Elegant callback. Using the duck as the medium for Pierce's emotional response after a long, charged silence lands well on multiple levels. It acknowledges Jim the Duck as real, uses Pierce's newly genuine connection to the cartoons, and the 'hacky duck' qualifier maintains the comedic distance even as Pierce is emotionally moved.

jokes.text: Pierce/Abed 'yelling' escalation: 'You shut up.' / 'You shut up.' / 'Now you shut up.' / 'You shut up.' / 'Oh, are we yelling? Are we yelling right now?' / 'Yelling! I'm yelling!'
jokes.setup: An emotionally charged scene between Pierce and Abed has reached a tipping point where both are genuinely flustered.
jokes.punchline: Their mutual 'you shut up' devolution is interrupted by Pierce's meta check-in ('Oh, are we yelling?') followed by their gleeful declaration of yelling — the confrontation collapses into absurd mutual acknowledgment.
jokes.explanation: The escalating 'you shut up' bit resolves with charming absurdity when Pierce breaks the fourth wall of their own argument to verify they're yelling, then both enthusiastically confirm it. The 'I'm yelling, I'm yelling, I'm yelling!' is a great button — genuine emotional release disguised as comedy. The callback 'you made me miss my movie' grounds it.

jokes.text: Pierce, quietly after the yelling: 'You made me miss my movie.'
jokes.setup: The yelling match has just ended. Pierce has had a genuine emotional breakthrough.
jokes.punchline: His post-catharsis complaint is not about the breakthrough but about the mundane consequence — 'You made me miss my movie' — which deflates the emotional seriousness with bathos.
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the Pierce/Abed storyline. The understatement works because Pierce IS the one who trapped Abed and prevented HIM from going to the movie — now delivering the same complaint in a small, quiet voice is both ironic and oddly touching. Economy is excellent.

jokes.text: Pierce attempting to bond over British comedy: 'Do you know Rimples and Splikket? They were the British Laurel and Hardy.' / Abed: 'Are they speaking English?'
jokes.setup: Pierce tries to share music/entertainment with Abed as a bonding gesture after their emotional confrontation.
jokes.punchline: He introduces 'Rimples and Splikket' — an obviously made-up British comedy duo — and then provides unnecessary historical context. Abed's 'Are they speaking English?' is the perfect flat response.
jokes.explanation: 'Rimples and Splikket' as a fake British duo name is funny on its face — the specificity of the clearly invented names. Pierce's pedantic historical footnote (the Oxford/Cambridge prime minister distinction) is a great character detail. Abed's flat 'Are they speaking English?' is the ideal deadpan button.

jokes.text: Do you like music? — Everyone likes music. What are you, a fish?
jokes.setup: Post-argument detente; Abed tries to establish common ground
jokes.punchline: Chang responds to the universal question ('do you like music?') with incredulous offense — 'What are you, a fish?' — implying only a fish wouldn't like music
jokes.explanation: 'What are you, a fish?' is a small gem of absurdist logic — fish as the designated music-haters of the animal kingdom. Perfect economy. It's the kind of line that makes you laugh without being able to fully explain why.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'Okay. '80s German techno it is.'
jokes.setup: Abed rejects Rimples and Splikket. Pierce has another option ready.
jokes.punchline: The alternative is '80s German techno — a sharp pivot from British Laurel and Hardy to a completely different cultural artifact, delivered as casually as offering a second coffee. Pierce's eclectic, bizarre taste is revealed.
jokes.explanation: Very economical Pierce character joke. The gap between Rimples & Splikket and '80s German techno as his two entertainment options says everything about his age, tastes, and disconnect. The casualness is key.

jokes.text: I've been defining myself with reactions to and from other people my whole life. Now I feel worthless just because I'm worthless in relation to my friends, which means they're not my friends.
jokes.setup: Jeff is in an existential spiral after his failed night at the bar
jokes.punchline: Jeff's logic is a perfectly constructed catch-22: he can't tell if his friends are friends because his self-worth is entirely relational
jokes.explanation: More of a character beat than a pure joke, but the recursive logic of Jeff's self-analysis is genuinely funny. 'I'm worthless in relation to my friends, which means they're not my friends' is the kind of Wingerism that shows the character's self-aware blindspot.

jokes.text: Pierce's existential speech: 'I've been defining myself with reactions to and from other people my whole life. Now I feel worthless just because I'm worthless in relation to my friends, which means they're not my friends.'
jokes.setup: Pierce opens up to Abed about his genuine feelings of isolation and worthlessness.
jokes.punchline: The logic collapses hilariously in real time: 'I feel worthless just because I'm worthless in relation to my friends, which means they're not my friends' — Pierce's reasoning simultaneously produces self-insight and self-sabotage, arriving at the wrong conclusion from true premises.
jokes.explanation: Pierce accidentally producing a logical non-sequitur from genuine self-reflection is very character-true. The 'which means they're not my friends' conclusion is both funny (bad logic) and sad (his real fear). This is the episode operating in its best mode: comedy and pathos simultaneously.

jokes.text: Pierce listing his friends: 'Well, there's my neighbor, Pat. I try to stay on his good side. I owe him money.'
jokes.setup: Abed asks Pierce who his friends are.
jokes.punchline: His first friend is defined entirely by a debt relationship — 'I try to stay on his good side. I owe him money.' — revealing that Pierce's social survival strategy is financial rather than emotional.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy. 'I try to stay on his good side. I owe him money.' is the entire joke in nine words. The relationship dynamic (maintaining 'friendship' through financial obligation) is both funny and revealing. Very Pierce.

jokes.text: Pierce tries to name Jeff as a friend, then Abed points out that Jeff and Pierce don't act like friends. Pierce: 'Yeah, I guess not so much.'
jokes.setup: Pierce names Jeff as someone he'd call a friend. Abed notes this doesn't match observed behavior.
jokes.punchline: Pierce's quiet concession — 'Yeah, I guess not so much' — after being confronted with the reality of his relationships is both funny and genuinely sad.
jokes.explanation: More of a character/emotional beat than a pure laugh, but the understatement lands. Pierce's resigned acceptance of his social reality is laced with sadness that makes it funnier-darker.

jokes.text: Abed's advice: '...the best lesson you could take away from it is that you are someone, even when you're by yourself.'
jokes.setup: Abed sends Pierce home after their deep conversation.
jokes.punchline: The irony that Abed — a character known for requiring constant external reference points and narrative structures to feel real — is delivering advice about self-sufficiency to Pierce. It's also played completely straight, which is funnier.
jokes.explanation: The meta-irony of Abed dispensing existential advice about being yourself when alone — when Abed famously processes everything through external cultural frameworks — adds a layer for attentive viewers. Played straight, which is the right call.

jokes.text: And please don't take offense at this, but thank you for not hitting on me. I was just vulnerable enough to do something really stupid.
jokes.setup: Jeff's companion thanks him for being platonic
jokes.punchline: She essentially tells Jeff to his face that she almost made a terrible mistake with him — 'really stupid' being the key indictment
jokes.explanation: Jeff not hitting on a vulnerable woman is played as an accomplishment worthy of thanks — a slight insult to Jeff's reputation. The 'really stupid' is the needle.

jokes.text: Pierce's parting comment: 'And please don't take offense at this, but thank you for not hitting on me. I was just vulnerable enough to do something really stupid.'
jokes.setup: Pierce says goodbye to Abed after their bonding session.
jokes.punchline: Pierce's thank-you is for NOT being hit on — implying that (a) he was worried Abed might, (b) he would have been susceptible in his vulnerable state, and (c) he's genuinely relieved to not have made 'a really stupid' decision.
jokes.explanation: Classic Pierce — his homophobic anxiety delivered as a sincere compliment, which makes it funnier and sadder simultaneously. The 'vulnerable enough to do something really stupid' implies a self-awareness about his own confusion that is unexpected. Very character-specific.

jokes.text: Pierce struggling with the steering wheel being on the wrong side of his British car.
jokes.setup: Pierce exits after their deep conversation and apparently tries to drive away.
jokes.punchline: The steering wheel is on the British side — Pierce apparently drives a right-hand-drive car in America — which is both a visual gag and a metaphor for Pierce being fundamentally positioned wrong in relation to everything.
jokes.explanation: Light but effective visual gag. Pierce's bafflement at a problem entirely of his own making is good character comedy. The metaphorical resonance (always on the wrong side) is a bonus for attentive viewers.

jokes.text: Jeff shows up at Abed's apartment with a script: 'It's a script I wrote about a cop on the edge. Troy thought it was hilarious. I didn't have the heart to tell him it wasn't a comedy.'
jokes.setup: Jeff unexpectedly shows up at Abed's apartment with a creative project.
jokes.punchline: His script is so unconsciously funny (or accidentally absurd) that Troy laughed throughout, thinking it was a comedy — and Jeff didn't correct him. This reveals both Jeff's creative pretension and Troy's good-natured obliviousness.
jokes.explanation: Economical and double-layered. Jeff's earnest dramatic script accidentally being hilarious, and his protecting both himself and Troy from the truth, is very Jeff. Good character integration for both mentioned characters.

jokes.text: 'It's time for Justice. Police Justice.' / Abed: 'Wait, the character's name is "Police Justice"?'
jokes.setup: Jeff reveals the title/tagline of his script.
jokes.punchline: The character's name is 'Police Justice' — an absurd, redundant, on-the-nose name that Jeff has apparently committed to with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. 'Police Justice' as a character name is the perfect parody of unself-aware macho thriller writing — Jeff's complete conviction in naming a cop 'Police Justice' is funny on its face. Abed's incredulous 'Wait, the character's name is Police Justice?' delivers the audience's reaction. Very clean structure, high quotability.

jokes.text: Jeff's realization at the bar — 'getting to third base with the wrong person' — followed by telling Britta she's a good friend, with Britta immediately clarifying 'you can't have sex with me.'
jokes.setup: Jeff finds Duncan at the bar and hints that he's realized something about his evening.
jokes.punchline: Britta pre-empts any romantic sentiment with 'you can't have sex with me' — immediately stripping the moment of any false depth. Then she offers a platonic drink alternative as if that's perfectly normal.
jokes.explanation: Britta's pre-emptive sex veto is very character-specific — she knows Jeff, she knows this dynamic, and she cuts to the chase. The 'not have sex, with anyone, together' proposal as friendship substitute is funny and oddly sweet.

jokes.text: Hey, handsome. This stool taken?
jokes.setup: Duncan has been struck out at the bar and sits dejectedly
jokes.punchline: Britta approaches Duncan — the person who spent the whole night trying to angle for her — with a flirtatious opening
jokes.explanation: Good ironic reversal — Duncan's entire scheme comes to fruition by accident. The 'Hey, handsome' is a sweet setup. It's more of a plot beat than a joke-joke.

jokes.text: How about we have these drinks and then not have sex, with anyone, together?
jokes.setup: Britta declines sex with Duncan; he has to respond
jokes.punchline: Duncan reframes their platonic evening as an activity — 'not have sex, with anyone, together' — using the syntax of an invitation
jokes.explanation: Syntactically inventive — 'not have sex, with anyone, together' is doing a lot of work. It recasts celibacy as a shared activity. The British-gentleman reframe of defeat into proposal is very Duncan. Good economy.

jokes.text: Jeff/Abed discussing the script: 'So a 9-millimeter's actually better than a 10-millimeter?' / 'Millimeter don't make no difference. Bullets just kinda kill you.' / Jeff: '"Bullets just kinda kill you." Are you quoting something? Can I use that?'
jokes.setup: Jeff and Abed are apparently now working on the script. Jeff asks a technical question.
jokes.punchline: Abed's response — 'Millimeter don't make no difference. Bullets just kinda kill you' — is so deadpan and definitively anti-action-movie that Jeff immediately wants to quote it. The collaborative dynamic reveals Jeff's creative limitations.
jokes.explanation: 'Bullets just kinda kill you' is a genuinely funny anti-action movie observation — it deflates the genre's obsession with gun spec. Jeff immediately trying to claim it as a quotable line is a great button on the joke.

jokes.text: Duncan to Britta: 'You left your handkerchief at my place last night.' / Jeff: 'We had a boys' night. A bottle of booze, an argument about sports cars. And I cut my hand trying to prove that I can whittle.' / Duncan: 'Me too.'
jokes.setup: Britta asks Duncan about the handkerchief. Jeff explains they had a boys' night.
jokes.punchline: The 'boys' night' consists of booze, sports car arguments, and both of them cutting their hands trying to whittle — the shared injury being the comedic peak, particularly 'Me too' confirming both men cut themselves at the same thing.
jokes.explanation: The whittling detail is perfect — the specificity of that particular failed masculine endeavor. 'Me too' as confirmation they both failed at the same thing is a good economical button.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'I had a monumental evening... by myself.'
jokes.setup: Everyone is sharing what they did the night before. The group is surprised Pierce had something notable.
jokes.punchline: 'By myself' — the pause followed by the deflating clarification — transforms what seemed like a brag into a statement of radical solitude, referencing the existential night he spent with Abed.
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback payoff. Pierce has internalized Abed's lesson and is reporting back — but doing it in a way that sounds sad and braggy simultaneously. The pause before 'by myself' is essential. Economy is very high.

jokes.text: Chang's ghost question to the committee: 'Do you guys believe in ghosts? And if you do, do you believe what those ghosts tell you about other ghosts?'
jokes.setup: Chang rejoins the committee meeting after his experience at the theater.
jokes.punchline: The question is absurdist on its face — the second clause ('what those ghosts tell you about other ghosts') adds a layer of deranged logic, suggesting Chang has been in a conversation with competing ghost factions.
jokes.explanation: One of the best Chang lines in the episode. The layered ghost epistemology — not just 'do you believe in ghosts' but 'do you believe what ghosts tell you about other ghosts' — is a genuinely clever absurdist construction. It implies Chang has been adjudicating competing ghost testimony, which is a great comic image.

jokes.text: Annie: 'Chang, you cannot be on the committee if you're going to be actively insane.'
jokes.setup: Chang is rambling about ghosts to the school committee.
jokes.punchline: 'Actively insane' — the qualifier 'actively' is key; it implies passive insanity might be tolerable, only the kinetic variety is disqualifying.
jokes.explanation: The 'actively' modifier is the entire joke and it works perfectly. Annie's pragmatic bureaucratic framing of insanity as a committee eligibility issue is very character-specific.

jokes.text: Chang: 'Huh, I guess we just didn't see you.' — after learning Britta was also at the benefit show.
jokes.setup: Britta mentions she was also at the theater the night before. Chang reveals he was there.
jokes.punchline: Chang's casual 'I guess we just didn't see you' — said entirely without self-awareness that he was busy accusing everyone of being a ghost.
jokes.explanation: Light callback. Chang's blithe explanation for not seeing Britta — implying normal social circumstances — when his actual night was dramatically different is funny but minor.

jokes.text: Post-committee scene: repeating the same ant allegory explanation as the opening — 'Well, the ants were people. The Queen Ant was an oil company.' — delivered by someone else entirely to someone who was apparently also at the show.
jokes.setup: The ant performance from the opening is referenced again.
jokes.punchline: The same rote explanation is delivered word-for-word again, implying this is the standard mandatory decoding everyone receives after the show — and perhaps that the performance is so obscure it requires this verbal user manual.
jokes.explanation: Good callback structure. The repetition implies the performance is so impenetrable it has an official explainer, and that this explainer gets deployed mechanically regardless of whether the person needs it. The near-verbatim repeat is the joke.

jokes.text: Chang: 'What if I don't exist?' / Group member: 'Oh, I got this. I had a very similar night last night. Go home, light some candles, and take a bath.' / Chang: 'Okay, coolsies.'
jokes.setup: Chang, rattled by the ghost situation, has an existential crisis.
jokes.punchline: Someone claims to have had a 'very similar' night and dispenses bath/candle advice as if this is the standard procedure for existential crises. Chang accepts this completely. 'Coolsies.'
jokes.explanation: The 'bath and candles' as the communally agreed solution to 'what if I don't exist' is a funny deflation of existential philosophy. 'Coolsies' from Chang is a perfect cap — his total acceptance of this advice without further probing.

jokes.text: What if I don't exist? — Oh, I got this. I had a very similar night last night. Go home, light some candles, and take a bath. — Okay, coolsies.
jokes.setup: Chang is having an existential crisis after the ghost theater
jokes.punchline: Jeff — who had his own existential crisis — dispenses advice with the confidence of an expert, and Chang accepts it with 'coolsies'
jokes.explanation: Jeff's breezy dispensation of candle-and-bath advice for existential crises is funny — he's essentially prescribing self-care as a philosophical solution. 'Coolsies' from Chang is an unexpected and endearing word choice.

jokes.text: [20-second gap — presumably a tag scene with no dialogue, Abed and Chang listening to 80s German techno or similar]
jokes.setup: Post-resolution beat between Abed and Chang after their bonding session
jokes.punchline: The extended silence — inferred from the 20:17-20:23 gap — is presumably a visual/tonal beat of two unlikely friends sitting together
jokes.explanation: Hard to score from transcript alone — this is likely a visual tag. Giving it a provisional low score as an inferred visual beat.

jokes.text: Jeff and Duncan's mutual 'Oh. Oh!' / 'No, no.' / 'Oh, okay. Yeah.' / various sounds of mutual social horror upon realizing they're about to invite each other to the same Tex-Mex restaurant.
jokes.setup: Jeff and Duncan run into each other on campus. Duncan mentions an off-campus lunch plan. Jeff mentions the same Tex-Mex place.
jokes.punchline: The sudden mutual realization — expressed through pure inarticulate sound — that they almost became lunch friends is played as social catastrophe. The extended series of 'oh's and 'no's is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Physical/verbal comedy built purely from mutual social dread. The extended sound-word exchange ('Oh. Oh!' 'No, no, no.') is a well-performed cringe beat. Character-specific to both: neither Jeff nor Duncan can commit to genuine friendship, especially with each other.

jokes.text: Hey! I was thinking off-campus lunch. What's that Tex-Mex place you mentioned? — Salsa Von Taco's? Read my mind!
jokes.setup: Jeff approaches Duncan with a lunch invitation — a callback to their bonding night
jokes.punchline: 'Salsa Von Taco's' is a magnificently absurd restaurant name delivered with complete enthusiasm
jokes.explanation: 'Salsa Von Taco's' is an inspired restaurant name — it sounds like a parody of Tex-Mex branding that would actually exist. 'Read my mind!' with full enthusiasm sells it. Good economy.

jokes.text: Duncan: 'I-I just don't like being left behind! My father got drunk in pubs and left me in my room with nothing!' / Jeff: 'So did mine!' / Duncan: 'Oh, why would he do that?' / Jeff: 'Why do they do that?' / Duncan: 'Why?'
jokes.setup: What started as social awkwardness about accidentally almost having lunch together suddenly explodes into a shared childhood trauma revelation.
jokes.punchline: The pivot from 'I don't want to have lunch with you' to 'MY FATHER LEFT ME' to genuine mutual grief ('Why do they do that? Why?') in under ten seconds is a stunning emotional escalation played for comedy — but also genuinely touching.
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode. The structure is perfect: social discomfort → one character's childhood wound → immediate mirroring by the other → mutual escalating grief delivered as rhythmic dialogue. The 'Why do they do that? WHY?' has the cadence of two people genuinely crying together while still being very funny. It simultaneously pays off both characters' emotional arcs (Duncan's alcoholic father-shaped neediness, Jeff's absent father). The speed of the escalation — from lunch awkwardness to shared abandonment trauma — is extraordinary. Structurally comparable to the vasectomy anchor example in its escalatory impact.

jokes.text: Duncan: 'I-I won't go to that Tex-Mex place.' / Jeff: 'Oh, that's all I wanted you to say.' / [shared moment of understanding]
jokes.setup: After the shared breakdown about their fathers, the conversation lands.
jokes.punchline: Jeff reveals the entire emotional outburst was resolved by simply NOT going to the same Tex-Mex place — 'that's all I wanted you to say' — reframing the childhood trauma revelation as a merely a means to that mundane end.
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the final scene. The childhood trauma outburst is immediately deflated to 'that's all I wanted you to say' — which retroactively makes the entire emotional moment a comically excessive means to a trivial social end. But the warmth underneath (they did connect, they DO share something) keeps it from being purely cold. The shared 'hmm?' is a lovely grace note. High structure and economy.

tmdb_overview: Jeff counsels a smitten Duncan on how to get a date with Britta but is developing feelings of his own. An angry Hickey tries to teach Abed a lesson.
insight: Season 5's weird turn yields 48 jokes in 44 minutes, balancing absurdist chaos with character-driven laughs.
